sections.title: D-1: Investigation
sections.summary: Introduces the Appendix D decision-tree process for investigating early-age cracking (cracking within the first 7 days, though some initiates at the slab bottom and surfaces later). Lists the 10 early-age cracking types, the 3-step investigation process, and Table D-1's type-to-possible-cause cross-reference for all 10 crack types.
sections.body: Determine the cause(s) of early-age cracking immediately, and implement action items to minimize or eliminate the causes or their effects before proceeding further with paving. Early-age cracking is typically classified as any cracking within the first seven days after concrete placement; however, some cracking may initiate at the slab bottom and not become visible for days or weeks. Table D-1 contains the types of cracks and possible causes and investigative techniques for each type of crack. The following are types of early-age cracking: plastic shrinkage cracking; random cracking (no orientation); longitudinal cracking; transverse cracking; corner cracking; cracks just ahead of sawing (pop-off cracks); later-age cracking (early-age slab bottom cracking propagating to surface); sympathy cracks; settlement cracks over dowel bars or tie bars; and re-entrant cracks. Note the following when early-age cracking develops: some cracking has an obvious cause and requires immediate corrective actions; marginal conditions can also cause cracking, and correcting one marginal condition may resolve an immediate problem but may not reduce the cracking potential for subsequent paving, so it is important to identify as many marginal conditions as possible and rectify as many as are under the control of the design engineer or the contractor as possible. The process of investigating early-age distress, for which the obvious cause is not readily apparent, involves the following steps: (1) gather relevant information; (2) identify if the distress manifests as isolated or systematic (widespread) occurrences, and if the distress is systematic, undertake a thorough review of the design features as well as all key construction procedures; and (3) work through an iteration of logical steps to pinpoint one or more causes, a process of elimination starting with obvious factors verified by field and laboratory personnel, with additional steps possibly requiring more rigorous evaluation of data, coring, and laboratory testing as causes are eliminated. Table D-1, Early Age Cracking Types/Possible Causes/Investigation, cross-references each of the ten cracking types against its listed possible causes. Plastic shrinkage cracking: high rate of evaporation (warm temperature, low humidity, windy), dry concrete mix, dry aggregates, late or inadequate curing, delay in finishing, temperature drop due to sudden cold front or rain, material incompatibility leading to higher shrinkage and delay in setting time, poor aggregate gradation (sand too fine; gap gradation). Random cracking (no orientation): slab-to-base bonding, concrete slab friction against rough base or concrete penetration into open-graded base, reflection cracking (from base cracking), late or inadequate curing, late sawing for prevailing conditions, shallow sawing of contraction joints in relation to actual slab thickness, poor aggregate gradation. Longitudinal cracking: late sawing for prevailing conditions, shallow sawing of the longitudinal contraction joint in relation to actual slab thickness, slabs too wide in relation to thickness and length, temperature drop due to sudden cold front or rain, misaligned or bonded dowels in adjacent longitudinal joints preventing cracked joints from functioning, excessive curling/warping, poor aggregate gradation, retarded concrete, early loading, infill lane restraints, late or inadequate curing, high-shrinkage concrete, slab-to-base bonding. Transverse cracking (partial or full width): late sawing for prevailing conditions, shallow sawing of transverse contraction joints in relation to actual slab thickness, slabs too long in relation to thickness and width, temperature drop due to sudden cold front or rain, misaligned or bonded dowels in adjacent transverse joints preventing cracked joints from functioning, excessive curling/warping, poor aggregate gradation, high-shrinkage concrete, early loading. Corner cracking: early loading, excessive curling and warping due to temperature changes or moisture loss, dowel bars too close to each other at transverse and longitudinal joints, late or inadequate curing, misaligned or bonded dowels in adjacent transverse joints. Cracks just ahead of sawing (pop-off cracks): late sawing for prevailing conditions, sawing against high wind. Later-age cracking (after about 7 days to about 60 days, or before aircraft loading): early-age slab bottom cracking finally becoming visible, frost heave, foundation settlement. Sympathy cracks: joints in a paved lane do not match joints in adjacent lanes, different joint cracking patterns in adjacent lanes, joints match in location but not in type. Settlement cracks over dowel or tie bars (not allowed on airfields): higher slump concrete, shallow dowel bars or tie bars, delay in setting time. Re-entrant cracks: use of odd-shaped slab panels, rigid penetrations (in-place structures). The printed table itself tabulates Cracking Type against Possible Causes; specific field and laboratory investigation techniques for narrowing down a cause (e.g., coring, distress mapping, records comparison) are the ones described in this section's three-step process and in the D-2 information-gathering checklist that follows.
key_points: Table D-1 lists 10 early-age cracking types: plastic shrinkage, random (no orientation), longitudinal, transverse, corner, cracks just ahead of sawing (pop-off), later-age (7-60 days or before aircraft loading), sympathy, settlement over dowel/tie bars, re-entrant.

Plastic shrinkage causes: high evaporation (warm/low humidity/windy), dry mix/aggregates, late/inadequate curing, delay in finishing, sudden cold front/rain, material incompatibility w/ high shrinkage & delayed set, poor aggregate gradation.

Random cracking causes: slab-to-base bonding, base friction/penetration into open-graded base, reflection cracking from base, late/inadequate curing, late or shallow sawing vs. slab thickness, poor aggregate gradation.

Longitudinal cracking causes: late/shallow sawing vs. thickness, slab too wide for thickness/length, cold front/rain, misaligned/bonded dowels blocking joint function, curling/warping, poor gradation, high-shrinkage/retarded concrete, early loading, infill lane restraints.

Transverse cracking causes: late/shallow sawing vs. thickness, slab too long for thickness/width, cold front/rain, misaligned/bonded dowels, curling/warping, poor aggregate gradation, high-shrinkage concrete, early loading.

Corner cracking causes: early loading, curling/warping from temperature or moisture change, dowels spaced too closely at joint intersections, late/inadequate curing, misaligned or bonded transverse dowels.
Cracks just ahead of sawing (pop-off) causes: late sawing for prevailing conditions, sawing against high wind.
Later-age cracking (7-60 days, or before aircraft loading) causes: early-age slab-bottom cracking becoming visible, frost heave, foundation settlement.
Sympathy crack causes: joints in a paved lane not matching adjacent-lane joints, differing joint cracking patterns between lanes, joints matching in location but not type.
Settlement cracks over dowel/tie bars (not allowed on airfields) causes: higher-slump concrete, shallow dowel/tie bar cover, delay in setting time.
Re-entrant crack causes: use of odd-shaped slab panels, rigid penetrations from in-place structures.

Investigation process: determine cause(s) immediately and act before further paving; distinguish isolated vs. systematic distress (systematic triggers full design/construction review); use elimination logic escalating to coring/lab testing.
tables: Table D-1: Early Age Cracking Types/Possible Causes/Investigation
sections.applicability: Applies at the outset of any investigation of early-age cracking (cracking within roughly the first 7 days, or slab-bottom cracking that surfaces later) in concrete pavement, to classify the crack type and identify candidate causes before data gathering begins.

sections.title: D-2: Gather Relevant Information
sections.summary: Introduces information gathering as step one of the early-age cracking investigation process. The needed information is organized into five categories addressed in the following sub-sections: design information, concrete mix information, environmental data, construction data, and other relevant data (distress mapping).
sections.body: Step one of the early-age cracking investigation process introduced in D-1 is to gather relevant information. This information is organized into five categories, addressed in the following sub-sections: design information (D-2.1), concrete mix information (D-2.2), environmental data (D-2.3), construction data (D-2.4), and other relevant data such as distress mapping (D-2.5). Collecting this information systematically, before further analysis, allows investigators to compare as-designed and as-built conditions against the timeline of the observed distress and to identify which possible causes from Table D-1 are actually present on the project.
key_points: Step one of the investigation process is to gather relevant information.
Information is organized into five categories: design, concrete mix, environmental, construction, and other relevant data.
Systematic information gathering supports comparison of as-designed versus as-built conditions against the distress timeline.
sections.applicability: Applies as the organizing step for the data-gathering phase (D-2.1 through D-2.5) of an early-age cracking investigation.

sections.title: D-2.1: Design Information
sections.summary: Design information to gather as part of an early-age cracking investigation: pavement thickness as designed, pavement thickness as constructed, transverse and longitudinal joint spacing, and base type.
sections.body: The design information to gather as part of investigating early-age cracking includes the pavement thickness as designed, the pavement thickness as actually constructed, the joint spacing (both transverse and longitudinal), and the base type used beneath the pavement. Comparing as-designed to as-constructed values is an important step in identifying whether a departure from the design contributed to the observed distress.
key_points: Record pavement thickness as designed.
Record pavement thickness as constructed.
Record transverse and longitudinal joint spacing.
Record base type.
sections.applicability: Applies to the design-information data-gathering step (D-2.1) of an early-age cracking investigation.

sections.title: D-2.2: Concrete Mix Information
sections.summary: Concrete mix information to gather as part of an early-age cracking investigation: cement type/source/grind history, supplementary cementitious materials (fly ash, slag) and content, aggregate gradation/type/source/amount and coarse aggregate coefficient of thermal expansion, and admixture manufacturer/type/dosage.
sections.body: The concrete mix information to gather includes cement type and source, and cement grind history (fresh grind versus not fresh grind); supplementary cementitious materials, including Type F fly ash source and slag source; cement content and supplementary cementitious material content (fly ash and slag); aggregate data, including gradation (uniform, gap graded, or other) with a gradation description, coarse aggregate type/source/amount, fine aggregate type/source/amount, and coarse aggregate coefficient of thermal expansion; and admixture manufacturer, type, and dosage for air-entraining admixtures, water reducers, and other admixtures.
key_points: Cement type, source, and grind history (fresh vs. not fresh grind).
Supplementary cementitious materials: Type F fly ash source, slag source, and their content.
Cement content.
Aggregate gradation type (uniform/gap graded/other) and gradation description.
Coarse aggregate type, source, amount, and coefficient of thermal expansion.
Fine aggregate type, source, and amount.
Admixture manufacturer, type, and dosage: air entraining, water reducer, other.
sections.applicability: Applies to the concrete mix data-gathering step (D-2.2) of an early-age cracking investigation.

sections.title: D-2.3: Environmental Data
sections.summary: Environmental data to gather as part of an early-age cracking investigation: weather conditions and temperature readings for the 3 days before paving through 14 days after (or present), hot/cold weather precautions taken, and rainfall history during and after paving.
sections.body: The environmental data to gather includes the weather conditions for the three days before paving through 14 days after paving (or through the present, whichever is earlier); the hot- or cold-weather precautions that were taken; temperature readings for the three days prior to paving through 14 days after paving or the present, whichever is earlier, with a table of readings attached; and the rainfall history during paving and for up to three days after concrete paving or through the present, whichever is earlier.
key_points: Weather conditions from 3 days before paving to 14 days after (or present), whichever is earlier.
Hot- or cold-weather precautions taken.
Temperature readings for the same window; attach a table of readings.
Rainfall history during paving and up to 3 days after (or present), whichever is earlier.
sections.applicability: Applies to the environmental data-gathering step (D-2.3) of an early-age cracking investigation.

sections.title: D-2.4: Construction Data
sections.summary: Construction data to gather as part of an early-age cracking investigation: paving history, bond-minimizing method for stabilized base, base surface condition, curing method, sawcut timing/depth (transverse and longitudinal), dowel alignment verification, and early-age loading history.
sections.body: The construction data to gather includes the paving history (start time, finish time, and curing time); the method used for minimizing bond between the pavement and a stabilized base; the base surface condition; the concrete curing method, including curing compound type and rate of application if used, and the number of days of moisture curing if applicable; the timing of sawcutting for both transverse and longitudinal joints; the depth of sawcut for both transverse and longitudinal joints, as specified and as actually measured (range); dowel alignment verification results; and the early-age loading history, including construction equipment loadings, drill rig loading, and other loading.
key_points: Paving history: start time, finish time, curing time.
Method used for minimizing bond for stabilized base; base surface condition.
Concrete curing method: curing compound type/rate (if used), days of moisture curing (if applicable).
Timing of sawcut for transverse and longitudinal joints.
Depth of sawcut (transverse and longitudinal) as specified versus actual range.
Dowel alignment verification results.
Early-age loading history: construction equipment loadings, drill rig loading, other.
sections.applicability: Applies to the construction data-gathering step (D-2.4) of an early-age cracking investigation.

sections.title: D-2.5: Other Relevant Data
sections.summary: Covers development and regular updating of distress maps (crack widths, ambient temperature at survey time) as the final data-gathering step of an early-age cracking investigation, used to determine whether distress is progressive and whether cracks are widening.
sections.body: Other relevant data to gather includes developing distress maps that estimate or measure crack widths and note the ambient temperature at the time of the distress survey. These maps should be updated regularly, every day or every few days, to determine whether the distress is progressive and whether the cracks are getting wider over time.
key_points: Develop distress maps; estimate or measure crack widths.
Note ambient temperature at the time of each distress survey.
Update distress maps regularly (daily or every few days) to track progression and widening.
sections.applicability: Applies to the final data-gathering step (D-2.5) of an early-age cracking investigation, used to track distress progression over time.
